claims.text: Replacing EAM+TI with MTP+FEP will reduce computational cost by more than 80%.
MTP+FEP will agree with baseline TOR-TILD within 0.5 meV/atom.
Maintaining the target accuracy requires the MTP to capture a solid-phase SRO stabilization energy of approximately 2-3 meV/atom.
Maintaining the target accuracy requires the MTP to capture electronic gap effects in the liquid.
The initial Ta-V-Cr-W alloy is a disordered BCC solid solution at 0 K.
The Ta-V-Cr-W system has a tendency toward Cr-V-rich segregation.
Short-range order stabilizes the solid by approximately 2-3 meV/atom.
A supercell containing more than 200 atoms is sufficient to capture SRO correlations without significant finite-size effects.
The 2000-2400 K range captures liquid-phase stability relevant to melting.
An MTP trained on TaVCrW DFT data can accurately reproduce the ab initio phase-space distribution.
Reproducing local atomic environments associated with SRO is necessary for an accurate free-energy landscape.
The MTP can retain electronic-structure accuracy, including the density-of-states gap near the Fermi level.
Accurate reproduction of the DFT phase-space distribution allows FEP to calculate free-energy differences from a limited number of samples.
FEP bypasses the slow convergence of TI when sampling the complex phase space of refractory high-entropy alloys.
The usual GGA-PBE/LDA underbinding and overbinding rules fail for V and Cr at 0 K.
Errors in PBE descriptions of V and Cr can propagate into the MTP training data and bias the predicted melting point.
Neglecting high-temperature magnetic fluctuations can introduce errors in the liquid free energy.
Magnetic contributions can shift melting points by tens of kelvin.
The method fails if the MTP training set omits configurations representing Cr-V segregation or relevant liquid electronic-gap shifts.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and predicted outcome describe melting-temperature accuracy using meV/atom, which is an energy unit, whereas the falsification rule applies the 0.5 meV/atom threshold to a free-energy difference. This makes the primary accuracy target internally ambiguous.
